---
title: "Institutions"
subtitle: "Who shapes Adamsville, and who is left out of the room"
---

Adamsville has many institutions, but they are not well connected to each other or to residents. The city and the agencies that fund development hold formal power, while churches, elders and personal relationships carry informal influence. From what I found, renters and young families have the least access to either.

## The institutional map

The diagram sorts Adamsville's institutions by the kind of power they hold. Formal power (rules and money) is at the top, the organizations that broker services and voice are in the middle, and residents are at the bottom. **Click any box** to see its role, power, incentive and how residents experience it; its connections stay highlighted. Solid lines are formal, regular relationships. Dashed lines are weak or occasional ones.

*Sources: interviews with Residents A and B (October 2026); City of Atlanta & TSW (2020); Invest Atlanta (2025a, 2025b); Atlanta News First (2022); Daniel (2025).*

## Incentives that pull in different directions

Several of the institutions I looked at want things that do not line up with what residents told me they need.

Invest Atlanta and the Hollowell/MLK Tax Allocation District (TAD) are the main source of development money along MLK Jr. Drive. The TAD, created in 2006, pays for projects using the growth in property tax revenue in the corridor, and its guidelines list "Adamsville Village" as a development site (Invest Atlanta, 2025b). The new food center was paid for this way, with $250,000 from the TAD and a $250,000 Invest Atlanta grant (Invest Atlanta, 2025a). The district is also part of the $5.1 billion Neighborhood Reinvestment Initiative that the mayor announced for south and west Atlanta in 2025 (WSB-TV, 2025). However, a TAD only produces money when property values go up, and for an older homeowner on a fixed income or a renter who is already cost-burdened, rising values are more of a risk than a benefit.

Atlanta Public Schools makes decisions mainly based on enrollment and cost. In 2022, APS reopened the old Margaret Fain Elementary building, which the Civic Club had called "the most important building in the community" in 1955, as a ninth-grade campus for Douglass High School (Atlanta News First, 2022). In late 2025, APS adopted a facilities plan that closes the building again to save about $500,000 a year (Daniel, 2025). Resident A had already noticed the difference: "the youth aren't as busy over here as much."

NPU-H is run by volunteers. Resident B called it "one of the most active" NPUs in the city, and when the food center opened, its chair, Khalifa S. Lee, pointed to the master plan: "We have in our master plan that we wanted food banks all across our area" (Andrews, 2025). The master plan process also shows how limited volunteer capacity is. Its 2019 community survey received 38 responses from an area of about 16,000 people, and steering committee attendance dropped from 13 to 5 between the first and second meetings (City of Atlanta & TSW, 2020, pp. 53–58). Resident A, who volunteers with the NPU, described the problem this way:

::: {.voice}
"The struggle is how do you engage community without like a incentive. Like, what's in it for me if I come to these meetings?"
<span class="who">Resident A, NPU-H volunteer, interview, October 16, 2026</span>
:::

## Who is represented, and what it costs those who are not

Both interviews suggest that the people who come to meetings and get listened to are mostly older homeowners. Resident B did not see this as a problem: "people respect their elders here… their voices are prioritized. And I actually think they should be."

Renters make up 54 percent of NPU-H households, but both residents described meetings attended mostly by the same homeowners and board members. Resident B, who is a working parent, said she usually joins while "multitasking" and that getting people to come is "like pulling teeth." The master plan recognizes this gap and includes a goal to "engage renters in the community and encourage them to stay" (City of Atlanta & TSW, 2020, p. 69). I think this affects which problems get attention. The issues that come up most at meetings, such as streetlights, signage and flooding, are mostly homeowner concerns, while two of the most striking figures in the census data, child poverty (44 percent) and renter cost burden (57 percent), rarely come up.

Resident B's experience with a sewage smell on her street shows how much personal connections can matter. The city fixed the problem only after a week of calls and left large holes in the road, and the holes were filled within a week after she mentioned them to a city official she knows personally. Resident A described a related gap: "the only people that really enforce anything in Adamsville are like code enforcers or police. There's no like middle person."

Investors and short-term rental owners are not part of the NPU at all, but they still shape the neighborhood. Resident A sees homes being renovated and listed "for rent, like Airbnb," which she said brings "strangers into the community" while pushing up property values. Research on metro Atlanta supports her concern. Brian An (2023) found that large investors bought up to 76 percent of homes for sale in some metro Atlanta neighborhoods between 2007 and 2016, mostly in majority-minority areas, and that they accounted for most of the decline in Black homeownership. In Fulton County, large corporate landlords were 68 percent more likely than small landlords to file evictions (Raymond et al., 2018). These owners do not come to NPU-H meetings, but their decisions affect who can afford to stay in Adamsville.
